steps.title: Key Context
steps.body: Elizabeth I was born on 7 September 1533 at Greenwich Palace, the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. Her path to the throne was far from straightforward - she was declared illegitimate, excluded from the succession, imprisoned in the Tower of London, and survived the dangerous reigns of her half-brother Edward VI and her half-sister Mary I. These experiences shaped her into a cautious, pragmatic, and deeply intelligent ruler.

steps.title: How Elizabeth's Early Life Shaped Her Rule
steps.body: The execution of her mother and her own imprisonment in the Tower taught Elizabeth the dangers of political life and the importance of caution. She learned to keep her thoughts private and never reveal her hand prematurely. Her humanist education gave her the confidence and intelligence to rule. The religious turmoil of Edward VI's Protestant reign and Mary I's Catholic restoration convinced her that religious extremism was dangerous - a lesson that directly influenced her Religious Settlement.

steps.title: Elizabeth's Approach
steps.body: Elizabeth wanted a moderate settlement that would satisfy most people. She was not a religious extremist - she famously said she had "no desire to make windows into men's souls." Her goal was political stability, not religious purity. The Settlement was designed to be a compromise: Protestant enough to satisfy most English people, but traditional enough to make Catholicism possible in practice.

steps.title: The Impact of the 1570 Excommunication
steps.body: Pope Pius V's bull Regnans in Excelsius (25 February 1570) transformed the Catholic challenge from a religious issue into a political one. By absolving Catholics of their allegiance to Elizabeth, the Pope effectively made being Catholic equivalent to being a potential traitor. This forced Elizabeth's government to treat Catholics as a security threat, leading to increasing persecution, fines for recusancy (refusing to attend Church of England services), and the execution of Catholic priests.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always use specific dates: Elizabeth born 1533 , accession 17 November 1558 , Religious Settlement 1559 , excommunication 1570 Know the difference between the Act of Supremacy (governing the Church) and the Act of Uniformity (governing worship) Explain the "middle way" clearly - it's a very common exam question For questions about challenges, discuss BOTH Catholic and Puritan opposition Remember that "Supreme Governor" was a deliberate compromise - not "Supreme Head" Link Elizabeth's early life experiences to her later decisions (caution, pragmatism) For 16+4 mark questions, write at least 3-4 developed paragraphs plus a conclusion
